parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 15. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman called Emma giving advice to a friend about canal boat holidays. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Tom: Hi Emma. Have you got a few minutes? You said you'd tell me about your canal boat holiday. Emma: Oh, hi Tom. Yes, of course. Are you thinking of going on one? Tom: Maybe. My parents' wedding anniversary is coming up, and my brother and I thought it might be a nice present for them. What's it actually like? Emma: Well, I loved it. I'd recommend it to anyone who wants to relax. You travel so slowly that there's no point rushing anywhere. You just watch the countryside go by, and stop at a pub when you feel like it. Tom: That sounds perfect for my parents. Is it hard to steer the boat? Emma: Not really. They give you a lesson before you set off, and you get the hang of it in about an hour. You don't need to be especially fit either, although opening the locks can be quite hard work. The main thing is that you have to be patient. Sometimes you have to wait for twenty minutes or more at a lock while other boats go through. Tom: My dad's very patient, so that won't be a problem. So where would you recommend? Emma: Well, one of the most famous is the Llangollen Canal, in north Wales. The scenery is amazing, and the highlight is a huge aqueduct that carries the canal right across a river valley, nearly forty metres above the water. It's quite scary the first time you go over it, because there's only a thin metal edge on one side. Tom: My mum's not great with heights. Emma: Then that might not be the best choice. It also gets very busy in the school holidays. The one we did was the Kennet and Avon Canal, in the south-west of England. We hired our boat from a company in Devizes. Tom: Sorry, where? Emma: Devizes. It's a market town in Wiltshire. It's spelt D, E, V, I, Z, E, S. Tom: Thanks. How long do you have to hire the boat for? Emma: Most people go for a week, which is what we did. But the minimum is three nights, if you just want a short break. And just outside Devizes, there's a famous flight of twenty-nine locks, one after the other, up a hill. It takes most of a day to get through them. Tom: Wow. What else is there to do along the way? Emma: Well, if you go west, the canal takes you all the way to Bath, so you could leave the boat for a day and go and see the Roman baths. They're amazing. There's also a lovely cathedral in Salisbury, but that's quite a long way from the canal. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Tom: When would be the best time to go? Emma: We went in September, and it was lovely and quiet, but it rained a lot. In July and August, it's very crowded. I think the best month is May. The weather's usually good, the countryside's very green, and the schools haven't broken up yet. Tom: OK. And how far can you travel in a day? Emma: Not very far. There's a speed limit of four miles an hour, and you have to slow down even more when you pass other boats, so most people only do about ten or twelve miles a day, especially if there are a lot of locks. Tom: That's really slow. Emma: That's the whole point. You're supposed to relax. Tom: Fair enough. What's it like inside the boat? Is there really room for four people? Emma: It's quite narrow, obviously, only about two metres wide, but ours had two bedrooms, a little kitchen and even a shower. It was surprisingly comfortable. Tom: That sounds better than I expected. And what about the cost? Emma: Well, it depends on the size of the boat and the time of year. For a boat that sleeps four people, for a week in May, we paid nine hundred and fifty pounds. That included fuel and a parking space for our car. If you go in the summer holidays, it can be twice that. Tom: That's not bad, if it's for four people. Is there anything else we'd need? Emma: Well, the boat has everything you need for cooking and sleeping. But I'd definitely recommend hiring some bikes as well. There's a path along the canal, so one person can ride ahead to get the next lock ready, or go to a shop to buy food. Tom: Good idea. My brother loves cycling. Did you have any problems at all? Emma: Only once, when we got stuck on some mud near the bank. A man on another boat helped to pull us off, and after that we kept to the middle of the canal. Tom: I'll warn my dad about that. Thanks, Emma. That's really helpful. Emma: No problem. I'll send you the name of the company we used. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a sports centre talking to parents about its after-school sports club. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Manager: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name's Jenny Clarke, and I'm the manager here at Highfield Sports Centre. I'm going to tell you about our after-school sports club, which I hope some of your children will be joining in September. Many of you will know the centre already, but for those who don't, we have a twenty-five metre pool, a sports hall, an indoor climbing wall and outdoor pitches. Manager: The club has actually been running for about eight years now, although it's grown a lot in that time. It runs every weekday during term time, from half past three until six o'clock. We collect children from four local primary schools in our minibus, so they don't need to make their own way here. Most children come two or three times a week, rather than every day, which is fine. We have a limit of sixty children at any one session, because of the number of staff we have, so it's a good idea to book as early as possible. Parents don't need to stay while their children are here, but you're very welcome to use the centre's café while you wait. All our staff are fully qualified and trained in first aid, and there is one member of staff for every eight children. Children are also divided into groups by age, so they are always with others of a similar age. Manager: Now, I know you'll want to know about costs. A full afternoon session, from half past three until six, costs eight pounds twenty-five per child. If you only need the first hour, until half past four, that costs four pounds fifty, and until five o'clock it's six pounds. There's a ten per cent discount for brothers and sisters. You can pay online each month or at reception, and if your child is ill, we'll refund the session as long as you tell us by midday. Manager: Food is something that parents often ask about. We ask you not to send snacks with your children, as we have a number of children with allergies. Instead, we provide fruit and a drink when the children arrive, and at five o'clock, everyone sits down to a proper hot meal, cooked in our own kitchen. The menus are on our website, and we can cater for special diets if you let us know in advance. Manager: During the school holidays, the club runs in a slightly different way. Instead of starting after school, it starts at half past eight in the morning and runs until five. Numbers stay the same, and it's still only for primary school children, but it's very popular, so again, do book early. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Manager: Now, let me tell you about some of the activities the children can do. As well as general games, we offer a number of special activities, and the children can choose which ones they'd like to try. Children who have homework can also do it in a quiet room with a member of staff, if their parents would like them to. Manager: Climbing is always very popular. We have an indoor climbing wall, and the children are taught by qualified instructors, and they must wear the helmets and harnesses that we provide. Because of the cost of the instructors and the equipment, there's a charge of three pounds per session on top of the normal fee, but most parents feel it's well worth it. Manager: Swimming takes place in our main pool on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Our lifeguards and swimming teachers are in the pool with the children, but we do need some parents to volunteer to help the younger children get changed. If you can spare an hour a week, please let us know, because without enough helpers, we can't run the sessions. The children also need to bring their own towel and swimming costume. Manager: Dance is something we added last year, and that was because so many of the children asked for it. We had a suggestion box in reception, and it was the most popular request by far. The classes include street dance and some traditional dances from around the world. Manager: Table tennis is new this term. We've just bought six new tables, thanks to a grant from the local council, and one of our staff used to play for the county, so the children will be in very good hands. Manager: And finally, archery. This is very exciting for the children, but for safety reasons, it's only open to children aged nine and over. Younger children will be able to try it when they're older. Unfortunately, we've had to stop offering trampolining this year, as the trampoline needs to be replaced, and we're still raising money for a new one. Right, are there any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear an events management student called Ben talking to his tutor, Dr Ahmed, about his work placement at a music festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Dr Ahmed: Come in, Ben. So, you've chosen your placement for the summer? Ben: Yes. I've decided on the Greenfields Music Festival. Dr Ahmed: Good choice. It's one of the biggest in the region. What made you choose that one? I know you were also considering the conference centre. Ben: Well, a lot of people think it'll be one long party, but that's not why. And it isn't near my home either. It's about two hours away. The main thing is that I've spent the whole year sitting in lecture rooms, and I really wanted a placement where I'd be working outside. Dr Ahmed: That makes sense. You'll certainly get plenty of fresh air. Now, I spoke to the festival manager last week, and she mentioned a few things. Safety is obviously her biggest concern. With thirty thousand people on site, the electrical equipment on the stages has to be checked every day, of course, and there's a first aid team. But what she stressed most was controlling the crowds in front of the main stages. If too many people push towards the front, it can become dangerous very quickly. Ben: Yes, I read about a festival abroad where people were injured because of that. Dr Ahmed: Exactly. So you'll be trained in how to spot the warning signs. She also talked about the local residents. The festival gives them free tickets, and some of them help out in the car parks. But the site is quite close to a village, and every year there are complaints about the noise, especially late at night. So part of your job may be dealing with those complaints, and some people can be quite angry. Ben: I'll try to stay polite. Dr Ahmed: Good. The other thing she mentioned is the schedule. Everything has to run exactly to time. Last year, there was a power cut for a few minutes, but they sorted that out very quickly. And the weather's never really a problem, because the stages are covered. What caused real difficulties was when one of the main bands turned up two hours late because their tour bus broke down. Every act after them had to be moved. Ben: That must have been a nightmare. Dr Ahmed: It was. The manager told me she didn't sleep for two days. Anyway, have you sorted out where you'll be staying? Ben: Yes, the festival provides tents for staff on a separate part of the site, and meals are included. Dr Ahmed: Good. Take plenty of warm clothes. It gets cold at night, even in the middle of summer. Ben: I will. My mum's already made me a list. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Dr Ahmed: Now, as part of your assessment, you'll need to reflect on the key skills of events management. Let's go through them. First of all, communication. Ben: I suppose that means speaking clearly to people. Dr Ahmed: Speaking clearly and listening carefully are important, of course, but it's more than that. People will judge you before you even open your mouth. If you turn up to meet a client in scruffy clothes, they won't take anything you say seriously. So you always need to look smart and professional. Ben: OK. I'll remember that. What about organisation? I'm quite good at making lists. Dr Ahmed: Lists are useful, but at a festival, things change all the time. A performer cancels, or the weather changes. You need to be able to change your plans at a moment's notice. That's the most important part of being organised in this business. Ben: Right. And time management? Dr Ahmed: When you're running late, and everyone's shouting at you, you have to keep calm, or at least look calm. If you panic, your whole team will panic too. So don't let people see that you're stressed. Ben: That might be difficult for me. What about creativity? I'd have thought that's about having big ideas. Dr Ahmed: Big ideas are great, but what really makes an event special is the small things. The signs, the lighting in the toilets, the flowers on the tables. Clients notice those details. Ben: Interesting. And leadership? I'm not sure I'm a natural leader. Dr Ahmed: You'll learn. Of course you should listen to experienced people. But in the end, a leader has to make decisions, and sometimes you have to go with your own judgement, even if others disagree. You have to believe in yourself. Ben: OK. And the last one is networking. Dr Ahmed: Networking is about building relationships. Don't just think about the event you're working on now. The people you meet at this festival could offer you a job in five years' time, so always think about where your career might take you. Ben: That's really useful. Thank you, Dr Ahmed. Dr Ahmed: You're welcome. Remember to keep a diary during the placement, because you'll need it when you write your report. And send me an email after the first week to let me know how it's going. Ben: I will. Thanks again. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a biology student giving a presentation on the mystery of where eels breed. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation, I've chosen what's sometimes called the eel question. The European eel is one of the most familiar fish in Europe. It lives in rivers, lakes and even ditches from Scandinavia to North Africa, and it has been an important food for centuries. In London, for example, jellied eels were once a popular dish among working people. And yet, for more than two thousand years, nobody knew where it came from, or how it reproduced. Student: The problem was that nobody had ever found an eel with eggs inside it, or even a baby eel. So people came up with some very strange ideas. The Greek philosopher Aristotle believed that eels simply appeared out of the wet earth, without parents. The Roman writer Pliny had a different theory. He thought that eels reproduced by rubbing themselves against rocks, and that the pieces of skin that came off grew into new eels. In later centuries, there was a popular belief in many parts of Europe that eels developed from horse hairs that had fallen into water. Student: Even when scientists began to study eels more carefully, the mystery remained. Part of the problem was that no one could find the eels' reproductive organs. In eighteen seventy-six, a young medical student in the Italian port of Trieste was given the task of solving this. He spent weeks cutting up around four hundred eels, looking for male organs, but he found nothing conclusive, and he later gave up biology altogether. His name was Sigmund Freud, and he went on to become rather more famous in a different field. Student: The first real clue came from a strange little fish known as a leptocephalus. It's flat and completely transparent, and shaped like a leaf, and for a long time it was thought to be a separate species. But in eighteen ninety-six, two Italian scientists kept some of these creatures in an aquarium and watched them change into young eels. So at last it was clear that eels start life as these leaf-shaped larvae. We now know that these larvae drift for many months, carried by ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream. Student: The next step was to find out where the larvae came from. This was the work of a Danish scientist, Johannes Schmidt. From nineteen oh four onwards, he spent nearly twenty years collecting larvae across the Atlantic. Because he couldn't afford his own research vessel for most of that time, he persuaded the captains of ordinary commercial ships to tow nets behind them as they crossed the ocean. He noticed that the further west he went, the smaller the larvae became, and the very smallest were found in the Sargasso Sea, a region of the western Atlantic near Bermuda. He concluded that this must be where the eels were born, a journey of around five thousand kilometres from the rivers of Europe. Student: But there was still no direct proof. Nobody had ever seen an adult eel in the Sargasso Sea, let alone watched them breed. It was only in twenty twenty-two that researchers were finally able to track adult European eels all the way there. They attached small satellite tags to eels released from the coast of the Azores, and followed their journey. The eels were released in the autumn, which is when adult eels normally leave European rivers. One surprising discovery was that the eels swim at great depths during the day, possibly to avoid predators, and come up closer to the surface at night. Student: Sadly, all of this research has become more urgent, because the European eel is now critically endangered. The number of young eels arriving in European rivers has fallen by more than ninety per cent since the nineteen eighties. There are several reasons for this, including dams that block their routes up rivers, pollution and disease. But one of the most serious threats is illegal trade. Young eels are caught in huge numbers and smuggled to Asia, where they are raised in farms and sold as food. Because we still can't breed eels in captivity, every eel that's eaten has been taken from the wild. So the eel question may finally have been answered, but unless we act quickly, the eel itself may not survive. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a sports centre talking to parents about its after-school sports club. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15. Manager: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. My name's Jenny Clarke, and I'm the manager here at Highfield Sports Centre. I'm going to tell you about our after-school sports club, which I hope some of your children will be joining in September. Many of you will know the centre already, but for those who don't, we have a twenty-five metre pool, a sports hall, an indoor climbing wall and outdoor pitches. Manager: The club has actually been running for about eight years now, although it's grown a lot in that time. It runs every weekday during term time, from half past three until six o'clock. We collect children from four local primary schools in our minibus, so they don't need to make their own way here. Most children come two or three times a week, rather than every day, which is fine. We have a limit of sixty children at any one session, because of the number of staff we have, so it's a good idea to book as early as possible. Parents don't need to stay while their children are here, but you're very welcome to use the centre's café while you wait. All our staff are fully qualified and trained in first aid, and there is one member of staff for every eight children. Children are also divided into groups by age, so they are always with others of a similar age. Manager: Now, I know you'll want to know about costs. A full afternoon session, from half past three until six, costs eight pounds twenty-five per child. If you only need the first hour, until half past four, that costs four pounds fifty, and until five o'clock it's six pounds. There's a ten per cent discount for brothers and sisters. You can pay online each month or at reception, and if your child is ill, we'll refund the session as long as you tell us by midday. Manager: Food is something that parents often ask about. We ask you not to send snacks with your children, as we have a number of children with allergies. Instead, we provide fruit and a drink when the children arrive, and at five o'clock, everyone sits down to a proper hot meal, cooked in our own kitchen. The menus are on our website, and we can cater for special diets if you let us know in advance. Manager: During the school holidays, the club runs in a slightly different way. Instead of starting after school, it starts at half past eight in the morning and runs until five. Numbers stay the same, and it's still only for primary school children, but it's very popular, so again, do book early. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20. Manager: Now, let me tell you about some of the activities the children can do. As well as general games, we offer a number of special activities, and the children can choose which ones they'd like to try. Children who have homework can also do it in a quiet room with a member of staff, if their parents would like them to. Manager: Climbing is always very popular. We have an indoor climbing wall, and the children are taught by qualified instructors, and they must wear the helmets and harnesses that we provide. Because of the cost of the instructors and the equipment, there's a charge of three pounds per session on top of the normal fee, but most parents feel it's well worth it. Manager: Swimming takes place in our main pool on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Our lifeguards and swimming teachers are in the pool with the children, but we do need some parents to volunteer to help the younger children get changed. If you can spare an hour a week, please let us know, because without enough helpers, we can't run the sessions. The children also need to bring their own towel and swimming costume. Manager: Dance is something we added last year, and that was because so many of the children asked for it. We had a suggestion box in reception, and it was the most popular request by far. The classes include street dance and some traditional dances from around the world. Manager: Table tennis is new this term. We've just bought six new tables, thanks to a grant from the local council, and one of our staff used to play for the county, so the children will be in very good hands. Manager: And finally, archery. This is very exciting for the children, but for safety reasons, it's only open to children aged nine and over. Younger children will be able to try it when they're older. Unfortunately, we've had to stop offering trampolining this year, as the trampoline needs to be replaced, and we're still raising money for a new one. Right, are there any questions? That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear an events management student called Ben talking to his tutor, Dr Ahmed, about his work placement at a music festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Dr Ahmed: Come in, Ben. So, you've chosen your placement for the summer? Ben: Yes. I've decided on the Greenfields Music Festival. Dr Ahmed: Good choice. It's one of the biggest in the region. What made you choose that one? I know you were also considering the conference centre. Ben: Well, a lot of people think it'll be one long party, but that's not why. And it isn't near my home either. It's about two hours away. The main thing is that I've spent the whole year sitting in lecture rooms, and I really wanted a placement where I'd be working outside. Dr Ahmed: That makes sense. You'll certainly get plenty of fresh air. Now, I spoke to the festival manager last week, and she mentioned a few things. Safety is obviously her biggest concern. With thirty thousand people on site, the electrical equipment on the stages has to be checked every day, of course, and there's a first aid team. But what she stressed most was controlling the crowds in front of the main stages. If too many people push towards the front, it can become dangerous very quickly. Ben: Yes, I read about a festival abroad where people were injured because of that. Dr Ahmed: Exactly. So you'll be trained in how to spot the warning signs. She also talked about the local residents. The festival gives them free tickets, and some of them help out in the car parks. But the site is quite close to a village, and every year there are complaints about the noise, especially late at night. So part of your job may be dealing with those complaints, and some people can be quite angry. Ben: I'll try to stay polite. Dr Ahmed: Good. The other thing she mentioned is the schedule. Everything has to run exactly to time. Last year, there was a power cut for a few minutes, but they sorted that out very quickly. And the weather's never really a problem, because the stages are covered. What caused real difficulties was when one of the main bands turned up two hours late because their tour bus broke down. Every act after them had to be moved. Ben: That must have been a nightmare. Dr Ahmed: It was. The manager told me she didn't sleep for two days. Anyway, have you sorted out where you'll be staying? Ben: Yes, the festival provides tents for staff on a separate part of the site, and meals are included. Dr Ahmed: Good. Take plenty of warm clothes. It gets cold at night, even in the middle of summer. Ben: I will. My mum's already made me a list. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Dr Ahmed: Now, as part of your assessment, you'll need to reflect on the key skills of events management. Let's go through them. First of all, communication. Ben: I suppose that means speaking clearly to people. Dr Ahmed: Speaking clearly and listening carefully are important, of course, but it's more than that. People will judge you before you even open your mouth. If you turn up to meet a client in scruffy clothes, they won't take anything you say seriously. So you always need to look smart and professional. Ben: OK. I'll remember that. What about organisation? I'm quite good at making lists. Dr Ahmed: Lists are useful, but at a festival, things change all the time. A performer cancels, or the weather changes. You need to be able to change your plans at a moment's notice. That's the most important part of being organised in this business. Ben: Right. And time management? Dr Ahmed: When you're running late, and everyone's shouting at you, you have to keep calm, or at least look calm. If you panic, your whole team will panic too. So don't let people see that you're stressed. Ben: That might be difficult for me. What about creativity? I'd have thought that's about having big ideas. Dr Ahmed: Big ideas are great, but what really makes an event special is the small things. The signs, the lighting in the toilets, the flowers on the tables. Clients notice those details. Ben: Interesting. And leadership? I'm not sure I'm a natural leader. Dr Ahmed: You'll learn. Of course you should listen to experienced people. But in the end, a leader has to make decisions, and sometimes you have to go with your own judgement, even if others disagree. You have to believe in yourself. Ben: OK. And the last one is networking. Dr Ahmed: Networking is about building relationships. Don't just think about the event you're working on now. The people you meet at this festival could offer you a job in five years' time, so always think about where your career might take you. Ben: That's really useful. Thank you, Dr Ahmed. Dr Ahmed: You're welcome. Remember to keep a diary during the placement, because you'll need it when you write your report. And send me an email after the first week to let me know how it's going. Ben: I will. Thanks again. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a biology student giving a presentation on the mystery of where eels breed. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation, I've chosen what's sometimes called the eel question. The European eel is one of the most familiar fish in Europe. It lives in rivers, lakes and even ditches from Scandinavia to North Africa, and it has been an important food for centuries. In London, for example, jellied eels were once a popular dish among working people. And yet, for more than two thousand years, nobody knew where it came from, or how it reproduced. Student: The problem was that nobody had ever found an eel with eggs inside it, or even a baby eel. So people came up with some very strange ideas. The Greek philosopher Aristotle believed that eels simply appeared out of the wet earth, without parents. The Roman writer Pliny had a different theory. He thought that eels reproduced by rubbing themselves against rocks, and that the pieces of skin that came off grew into new eels. In later centuries, there was a popular belief in many parts of Europe that eels developed from horse hairs that had fallen into water. Student: Even when scientists began to study eels more carefully, the mystery remained. Part of the problem was that no one could find the eels' reproductive organs. In eighteen seventy-six, a young medical student in the Italian port of Trieste was given the task of solving this. He spent weeks cutting up around four hundred eels, looking for male organs, but he found nothing conclusive, and he later gave up biology altogether. His name was Sigmund Freud, and he went on to become rather more famous in a different field. Student: The first real clue came from a strange little fish known as a leptocephalus. It's flat and completely transparent, and shaped like a leaf, and for a long time it was thought to be a separate species. But in eighteen ninety-six, two Italian scientists kept some of these creatures in an aquarium and watched them change into young eels. So at last it was clear that eels start life as these leaf-shaped larvae. We now know that these larvae drift for many months, carried by ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream. Student: The next step was to find out where the larvae came from. This was the work of a Danish scientist, Johannes Schmidt. From nineteen oh four onwards, he spent nearly twenty years collecting larvae across the Atlantic. Because he couldn't afford his own research vessel for most of that time, he persuaded the captains of ordinary commercial ships to tow nets behind them as they crossed the ocean. He noticed that the further west he went, the smaller the larvae became, and the very smallest were found in the Sargasso Sea, a region of the western Atlantic near Bermuda. He concluded that this must be where the eels were born, a journey of around five thousand kilometres from the rivers of Europe. Student: But there was still no direct proof. Nobody had ever seen an adult eel in the Sargasso Sea, let alone watched them breed. It was only in twenty twenty-two that researchers were finally able to track adult European eels all the way there. They attached small satellite tags to eels released from the coast of the Azores, and followed their journey. The eels were released in the autumn, which is when adult eels normally leave European rivers. One surprising discovery was that the eels swim at great depths during the day, possibly to avoid predators, and come up closer to the surface at night. Student: Sadly, all of this research has become more urgent, because the European eel is now critically endangered. The number of young eels arriving in European rivers has fallen by more than ninety per cent since the nineteen eighties. There are several reasons for this, including dams that block their routes up rivers, pollution and disease. But one of the most serious threats is illegal trade. Young eels are caught in huge numbers and smuggled to Asia, where they are raised in farms and sold as food. Because we still can't breed eels in captivity, every eel that's eaten has been taken from the wild. So the eel question may finally have been answered, but unless we act quickly, the eel itself may not survive. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
